page_heading: Got a Lease Offer or a Letter About Your Minerals?
page_subtitle: Before you sign anything, we will read the record and tell you in plain English what you own and what the offer says.
meta_description: Help for Pennsylvania mineral owners with lease offers, inherited mineral rights, division orders and royalty questions, from Certified Professional Landmen.
intro:
Has a company asked to lease your minerals, run a line across your land, or have you sign a division order (the form that sets your share before royalty checks start)? You do not have to figure it out alone.

We are Certified Professional Landmen, and we read the public record for a living. We tell you what you own, what the document in front of you says, and what the record leaves unsettled.

services.title: Mineral ownership reports
services.description: A written report of what the public record shows you own and how it came to you. It also shows where the chain of title (each transfer from one owner to the next) has gaps.

services.title: Heirship research
services.description: Tracing a share through estates and probate when a relative's ownership was never passed down on paper.

choices.label: A lease offer
situations: I got a lease offer and want to understand it before I answer.
choices.what: A company is asking for the right to drill for and produce oil and gas under your land for a set term, in return for a bonus paid up front and a royalty on what is produced. It usually arrives as a printed lease, an addendum and a memorandum for recording, and the addendum often overrides the printed form.
checks: The royalty rate. Pennsylvania law sets the floor at one-eighth (12.5%), so check the exact figure.
Post-production costs: whether the company may subtract gathering, processing and transport costs before paying you.
The primary term, and any option to extend it on terms set today.
The acres and the share the bonus is based on, against what the record shows you own.
choices.send: The whole packet: the lease, any addendum or exhibit, the memorandum and the bonus paperwork, plus the county. A photo of each page is fine.
choices.more_label: Read what is in a lease offer

choices.label: A division order or royalty check
situations: A division order came in the mail and I don't know if the decimal is right.
My royalty check stopped, dropped, or looks wrong.
choices.what: A division order is the form an operator sends before royalty payments start. It states your share of the well as a decimal, and your checks follow that number.
checks: The decimal. It should match your share of the unit, worked out from your share, your acres, the unit size and your royalty rate.
The name and the land: the owner and the tract should match your deed, or the estate the interest came through.
The well or unit it names, and the date it takes effect.
If a check stopped or dropped: the well, the volumes and the deductions on the statement, against earlier months.
choices.send: The division order, or the royalty statement that looks wrong, plus your deed or the estate papers and the county.
choices.prefill: A division order or a royalty statement.

choices.label: A pipeline, right-of-way, solar or wind letter
situations: A pipeline, solar, or wind company contacted me about my land.
choices.what: A company wants to use the surface of your land: a strip for a pipeline or power line (a right-of-way, also called an easement), or acreage leased for solar panels or wind turbines. These agreements usually run for many years and stay with the land when it is sold.
checks: Where on your land: the route or the area, its width, and any temporary work space.
How long it lasts, and whether the company can hand it to another company.
What is paid and when, including damage to crops, timber, fences and water.
Whether the company has to put the land back the way it was when the work is done.
choices.send: The letter and anything that came with it, such as an agreement or a map, plus the county and the tax parcel number if you have it.
choices.prefill: A pipeline, right-of-way, solar or wind letter.

choices.label: A letter about an estate, heirs or inheritance
situations: I inherited mineral rights and I'm not sure what I own.
choices.what: Mineral rights pass through wills and estates like any other property, and a share can be split again every generation. A letter like this often means a company has found your family's name in the record and is working out who owns that share now.
checks: Whose estate or which relative it names, and the county the land is in.
The share it says you hold, and how it says that share came to you.
Whether the estate was ever settled, or a transfer was never filed. Gaps like that are common in inherited interests.
Anything it asks you to sign, such as a sworn statement about your family (an affidavit of heirship).
choices.send: The letter, any deeds, wills or probate papers you have, and the names and dates of the relatives the interest came through.
choices.prefill: A letter about an estate, heirs or an inheritance.

choices.label: An offer to buy your minerals or land
situations: I'm buying or selling land and need to know about the minerals.
choices.what: Someone wants to buy your mineral rights, your royalty or the land itself. A sale is permanent, and what you would be selling depends on what you actually own, which can be more or less than the offer assumes.
checks: Exactly what it covers: all minerals, only oil and gas, or only royalty, and at which depths.
The acres and the share it assumes you own, against what the record shows.
Whether the land and the minerals are owned separately. In Pennsylvania they often are.
If you are the one buying land: whether the minerals come with it, or were kept back in an old deed.
choices.send: The offer or the purchase agreement, your deed and the county. If you are buying, the deed or listing you were given.
choices.prefill: An offer to buy minerals or land.

choices.label: Not sure what it is
choices.what: Companies send many kinds of letters and forms about land and minerals, and the wording does not always make clear what they are asking for. Reading them is what we do every day.
checks: Who sent it, and whether it asks you to sign, return or record anything.
Any date it gives for a reply.
The land it describes: the county, township, acres or tax parcel.
Any number for your share, such as a fraction or a decimal.
choices.send: A photo or copy of every page, and the county. That is enough to start.
choices.prefill: I'm not sure what it is.

lease_packet.label: Lease Offers
lease_packet.headline: What Is in a Lease Offer
lease_packet.intro: A lease offer usually comes as a printed lease, an addendum and a memorandum for recording. The addendum often overrides the printed form, and a few clauses decide most of what the lease is worth to you.

documents.title: The printed lease form
documents.text: The company's standard lease, usually several pages of small print. It sets out what you grant, for how long, your royalty and what the company may do on your land, in wording the company drafted.

documents.title: The addendum or exhibit
documents.text: Extra pages attached to the lease, sometimes called an addendum, rider or exhibit. They often change or override the printed form, so the terms that matter most are frequently here and the two have to be read together.

documents.title: The memorandum of lease
documents.text: A short document signed with the lease and filed with the county Recorder of Deeds (the office that keeps the land records), so the public record shows the lease exists. It names the parties, the land and the term but usually not the money, so check that its description of your land matches the lease.

documents.title: The bonus payment paperwork
documents.text: The draft, order or other paperwork for the bonus, the money paid up front for signing. Read when it pays and on what conditions, because some bonus drafts are paid only after the company has checked title.

terms.title: Royalty rate
terms.text: Your share of production, written as a fraction or a percentage. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets the floor at one-eighth (12.5%), so check the exact figure and whether it applies to oil, gas and every other product the lease covers.

terms.title: Post-production costs and deductions
terms.text: Whether the company may subtract the cost of gathering, processing, compressing and transporting gas before paying your royalty. Look at how the royalty is calculated and what may be deducted, because it can make a large difference to what you are actually paid.

terms.title: Primary term and extension
terms.text: How long the company has to start drilling or producing before the lease ends on its own. Look for an option to extend or renew, which can add years on terms set today.

terms.title: Bonus per acre
terms.text: The up-front payment for signing, usually figured per net mineral acre: the acres you own, scaled by your share, so a one-half interest in 50 acres is 25 net mineral acres. Check the acreage it is based on against what the record shows you own, and when and how it is paid.

terms.title: Pooling and unitization
terms.text: Whether the company may combine your acreage with neighboring tracts into one drilling unit (pooling, or unitization) and share production by acreage. Look at any limits on unit size and how your share of the unit is worked out.

terms.title: Pugh clause
terms.text: Releases the land or depths outside a producing unit once the primary term ends. Without one, a well on part of your tract can hold the whole lease.

terms.title: Shut-in clause
terms.text: A shut-in well is drilled and able to produce but is not selling, often while it waits for a pipeline. This clause lets the company keep the lease in force by paying a shut-in royalty during that time. Look at the amount and how long the lease can be held this way.

terms.title: Depth limits
terms.text: Whether the lease covers every formation or only certain depths. Depths left out of the lease stay yours to lease separately.

terms.title: Surface use and damages
terms.text: Where the company may put roads, well pads, pipelines and equipment, and what it pays for damage to crops, timber, fences and water. Look for setbacks from your house and water supply, and a duty to restore the land.

lease_packet.closing: We check the offer against the record and go through it with you, clause by clause, before you answer. Call us, or send it over.

faq.question: What will it cost?
faq.answer: It depends on what the record holds. The main factors are how many tracts are involved, how far back the title has to be run, and whether there are heirship questions or missing or unclear records along the way. It also depends on whether you need a written report you can hand to someone else or just an informal read of what you have. Send us the details and we will tell you what the work involves, and we keep you posted if the record turns up something that changes it.

faq.question: How long does this take?
faq.answer: It depends on the county and on how far back the chain has to be run. Some counties have everything indexed and searchable online. Others mean a day at the courthouse and records filed under a name spelled three different ways. Heirship questions and missing records add time too. Once we know the tract and the county we will tell you what the work involves, and we keep you posted as it goes, especially if the record turns up something that changes the picture.

faq.question: I inherited minerals and I am not sure what I own. Can you find out?
faq.answer: Usually, yes, and it is ordinary work for us. We trace the interest back through the deeds and the probate records and report what the record supports. Inherited interests often have gaps: an estate that was never settled, or a transfer that was never filed. Sometimes the gap is several generations back, in a county nobody thought to check. Those gaps are exactly what we go looking for.

faq.question: What is a division order?
faq.answer: The form an operator sends before royalty payments start. It states your share of the well as a decimal, and your checks follow that number, so it is worth checking against the record before you sign and return it. We can tell you how the decimal was worked out and whether it matches what the record shows you own.

faq.question: What does a landman actually do?
faq.answer: A landman works out who owns what, using the public record. Most of that work happens at the county courthouse. We go through deeds, leases, wills, probate files and court records, follow an interest through every transfer, and write up what the record shows. Certified Professional Landman is the credential the American Association of Professional Landmen issues for that work.

faq.question: Can you tell me whether the offer I received is a fair price?
faq.answer: We can tell you whether the offer describes the right tract, whether the interest it credits you with matches what the record shows, and which of the terms will matter most over the life of the agreement. Our job is to make sure any decision you make is based on an accurate picture of what you actually own and what the offer actually says. Send us the offer and we will go through it with you clause by clause.

faq.question: What do you need from me to get started?
faq.answer: Whatever you already have. The offer or division order if you were sent one, any deeds, wills or probate paperwork sitting in a drawer, and the county and state the property is in. If all you have is a letter and a rough idea of where the land is, that is still enough for a first conversation.

pennsylvania_note:
- Surface and minerals are often owned separately here, and old deeds often split off the oil, gas or coal.
- Deeds and leases are filed with the county Recorder of Deeds, the office that keeps the land records. Wills go to the county Register of Wills, and estates are settled in the Orphans' Court, the county court that handles estates.
- Under the Dunham Rule, a deed that reserves "minerals" is presumed not to include oil and gas unless it names them. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reaffirmed this in *Butler v. Charles Powers Estate* (2013).
- Pennsylvania has no general law that lets a company pool your Marcellus acreage into a unit without your consent (called forced pooling).
- By law (the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, 58 P.S. § 33.3), an oil and gas lease must guarantee the owner at least a one-eighth (12.5%) royalty.

This is general information, not legal advice. Send us your deed or lease and we will tell you what the record shows for your own tract.
conflict_note: We also take leases for oil and gas companies. If we are already working for the company on the other side of your offer, we will not review it for you, and we will tell you so at the start. The AAPL Code of Ethics requires us to disclose conflicts like this.
disclaimer: We are landmen, not attorneys, so what we give you is the public record, not legal advice. If anything in your file calls for more than that, we will tell you when we go through it with you.
